title: How do sealed classes/interfaces extend OOP's inheritance by giving the supertype CONTROL over its hierarchy (permits only listed subtypes, each must be final/sealed/non-sealed), and how does this enable exhaustive pattern matching in switch?
shortTitle: What are sealed classes and interfaces?

s1_definition.profdef: A `sealed` class/interface restricts which classes can extend/implement it using the `permits` clause. `sealed interface PaymentChannel permits Neft, Upi, Rtgs {}` — ONLY Neft, Upi, and Rtgs can implement PaymentChannel. Any other class trying to implement it gets a COMPILE ERROR. Each permitted subtype must be one of: `final` (no further extension), `sealed` (controlled further extension), or `non-sealed` (open for anyone to extend). The key benefit: the compiler KNOWS all possible subtypes at compile time. This enables EXHAUSTIVE pattern matching in switch — the compiler verifies all subtypes are handled, NO default needed. Adding a new subtype → compile error in every switch that doesn't handle it.
s1_definition.analogy: Before sealed: the PaymentChannel interface was OPEN — anyone could create `BitcoinChannel implements PaymentChannel` without the bank's approval. With sealed: the bank's PaymentChannel says "ONLY Neft, Upi, and Rtgs are approved channels." If someone tries to create BitcoinChannel → COMPILE ERROR. The system's switch statement handles exactly 3 channels — no surprise implementations. Adding ImpsChannel to the permits list → every switch that processes payment channels gets a compile error until it handles IMPS.
s1_definition.oneliner: sealed = parent CONTROLS which children exist (permits list). Children must be final/sealed/non-sealed. Enables EXHAUSTIVE switch — compiler ensures all subtypes handled. No default needed. New subtype → compile error everywhere.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A `sealed` class/interface restricts which classes can extend/implement it using the `permits` clause. `sealed interface PaymentChannel permits Neft, Upi, Rtgs {}` — ONLY Neft, Upi, and Rtgs can implement PaymentChannel. Any other class trying to implement it gets a COMPILE ERROR. Each permitted subtype must be one of: `final` (no further extension), `sealed` (controlled further extension), or `non-sealed` (open for anyone to extend). The key benefit: the compiler KNOWS all possible subtypes at compile time. This enables EXHAUSTIVE pattern matching in switch — the compiler verifies all subtypes are handled, NO default needed. Adding a new subtype → compile error in every switch that doesn't handle it.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Before sealed: the PaymentChannel interface was OPEN — anyone could create `BitcoinChannel implements PaymentChannel` without the bank's approval. With sealed: the bank's PaymentChannel says "ONLY Neft, Upi, and Rtgs are approved channels." If someone tries to create BitcoinChannel → COMPILE ERROR. The system's switch statement handles exactly 3 channels — no surprise implementations. Adding ImpsChannel to the permits list → every switch that processes payment channels gets a compile error until it handles IMPS.

**One line to remember:** sealed = parent CONTROLS which children exist (permits list). Children must be final/sealed/non-sealed. Enables EXHAUSTIVE switch — compiler ensures all subtypes handled. No default needed. New subtype → compile error everywhere.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's payment routing service has a PaymentChannel interface.** Without sealed: a vendor created `CryptoChannel implements PaymentChannel` — the system's switch had a default that logged "unknown channel" and silently DROPPED the payment. Rs.15 lakh lost. With sealed: only Neft, Upi, Rtgs are permitted. CryptoChannel → compile error. The switch has NO default — compiler guarantees all channels handled. When the bank adds ImpsChannel to the permits list, every switch in the codebase gets a compile error until IMPS is handled. Zero silent drops.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** `sealed interface PaymentChannel permits NeftChannel, UpiChannel, RtgsChannel` — compiler records: ONLY these 3 types can implement PaymentChannel. Any other → compile error.

**Step 2.** `switch (channel) { case NeftChannel → ... case UpiChannel → ... case RtgsChannel → ... }` — compiler checks: all 3 permitted types handled? YES → no default needed. Exhaustive!

**Step 3.** Bank decides to add IMPS. Developer adds `ImpsChannel` to the permits list. EVERY switch on PaymentChannel in the codebase gets a compile error: "switch expression does not cover all possible input values." Developer MUST handle IMPS in every switch. Zero silent drops.

**Step 4.** sealed + records = `TransactionResult` with Success/Failure/Pending records. Switch on result: all 3 cases handled without default. Adding a new result type (Timeout) → compile errors force handling everywhere.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Sealed classes/interfaces (Java 17) give the supertype CONTROL over its hierarchy using the `permits` clause. `sealed interface PaymentChannel permits Neft, Upi, Rtgs` — only these 3 types can implement it. Any other class attempting to implement PaymentChannel gets a compile error. Each permitted subtype must be `final` (no further extension), `sealed` (controlled further), or `non-sealed` (open — escape hatch). This is different from a regular abstract class/interface where ANY class can extend/implement it.

The key benefit is EXHAUSTIVE pattern matching in switch (Java 21). The compiler KNOWS all possible subtypes → it verifies every case is handled → no default clause needed. Without sealed: the switch needs a default because unknown implementations could exist. With sealed: adding a new subtype (ImpsChannel) to the permits list causes compile errors in EVERY switch statement that doesn't handle it — zero silent drops, zero missed cases.

In my payment router, sealed + records create algebraic data types: `TransactionResult` can ONLY be Success, Failure, or Pending. The switch destructures each record type and handles it exhaustively. If the team adds a `Timeout` result type, every switch on TransactionResult in the codebase immediately shows a compile error — forcing developers to handle the new case. This is the compile-time safety that sealed classes provide: the type hierarchy is a CLOSED set, and the compiler enforces complete handling.
